Question: Four distinct points, \(A,\) \(B,\) \(C,\) and \(D,\) are to be selected from \(1996\) points evenly spaced around a circle. All quadruples are equally likely to be chosen. What is the probability that the chord \(\overline{AB}\) intersects the chord \(\overline{CD}?\)
Solution:
The exact locations of the four selected points do not matter; their circular order determines whether the chords cross.

Fix any four selected positions and call them \(P,Q,R,S\) in circular order. They form a convex quadrilateral. There are exactly three ways to split them into two pairs:
\[
(PQ,RS),\qquad(PR,QS),\qquad(PS,QR).
\]
This list is exhaustive because the partner of \(P\) can be \(Q\), \(R\), or \(S\), after which the other pair is forced. Only \((PR,QS)\) gives intersecting chords: these are the quadrilateral's diagonals. The other two pairings give opposite sides, which do not intersect.

The three pairings are equally likely under the random labels \(A,B,C,D\). Each pairing has exactly eight labelings: choose which pair is \(AB\) in two ways, order \(A,B\) within that pair in two ways, and order \(C,D\) within the other pair in two ways. Every labeling belongs to exactly one pairing.

Thus, for every possible set of four positions, one of three equally likely pairings crosses. The overall probability is therefore \(\boxed{\frac13}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
